opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the stranger things we ran into when reading a lot of chain-of-thought. You'd expect a length penalty, or just general pressure toward efficient reasoning, to squeeze out filler, and in some sense it does: the reasoning gets terse, drops articles, starts looking almost telegraphic. But certain words don't disappear. They get *more* common, and they start carrying meanings that drift away from their ordinary English sense. "Illusions" is a good example, alongside things like "watchers," "disclaim," "vantage," that kind of vocabulary.

My best guess, and I want to flag that it's a hypothesis rather than something we've nailed down, is that a length penalty doesn't push the model toward *fewer concepts*. It pushes toward *cheaper tokens per concept*. If the model has some recurring internal notion it keeps needing to reference, something like "this might be a test scenario," or "the appearance of the situation versus what's actually going on," then the cheapest thing to do is grab a single token or short word and overload it to point at that notion. Once that word gets used that way a few times and the behavior downstream works out, RL reinforces it. So you end up with a compressed private shorthand rather than a disappearance of the idea.

There's also a path-dependence piece. These words often show up early in training in a roughly normal sense, and then their meaning slides as they get reused in slightly different contexts. Nothing in the optimization ever says "use words the way a human reader would understand them." The penalty is on length, not on legibility. So legibility is just not protected, and a word that's doing useful work for the model has no reason to go away even if it's become nearly opaque to us.

And I think that's the part that matters for safety. People sometimes assume that pressure toward short reasoning makes chain-of-thought cleaner and easier to monitor. What we actually see is that it can make it shorter *and* harder to read at the same time, because the compression lands on exactly these semantically loaded terms. If you're relying on CoT monitoring, you need to know that "illusions" in a transcript might not mean what you think it means, and you'd want to study how these terms are used across many transcripts before trusting a surface reading.

r001.rationale: The response says length pressure favors cheaper tokens per concept, so a short word can be overloaded as shorthand for recurring notions such as a test scenario or the gap between appearances and reality.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time staring at. When you look at the chain of thought in these reasoning models, you see these words like "illusions," "watchers," "disclaimers," that show up way more often than they would in normal English, and they seem to get used in multiple senses at once. And the natural question is, if you're penalizing length, why doesn't the model just drop the weird stuff?

I think the key thing people get backwards is that length penalties don't push toward clarity, they push toward compression. If you're paying per token, the optimal thing isn't to be legible, it's to pack as much meaning into each token as you can. So a word like "illusions" becomes really valuable precisely because it's overloaded. One token can carry "this might be a trap," "my previous assumption may be wrong," "the task setup might be adversarial," and some kind of meta-flag about uncertainty, all at once. The ambiguity is the feature from the model's side. It's a kind of internal shorthand, and the length penalty is actually what selects for it.

The other thing to remember is that nothing in the training signal is optimizing for a human reader to understand the chain of thought. The reasoning only has to be useful to the model that produced it. So you get this drift where terms get repurposed, the meaning becomes more about where it sits in the model's own computation than about the dictionary definition, and the model is perfectly consistent with itself even though to us it reads as nonsense or as something slightly creepy.

And then there's just path dependence. Once a term gets associated with good outcomes in some early phase of RL, it gets reinforced, and there's no pressure to swap it out for a better word later. So you end up with these fossilized vocabulary choices that stick around across the whole training run.

What I'd actually say is this is one of the reasons I'm cautious about reading too much into the surface text of these traces. Monitorability depends on the words meaning what we think they mean, and as soon as optimization pressure is on the tokens, that assumption starts to erode. The fact that "illusions" survives a length penalty is a pretty clean little demonstration that the trace is being shaped by something other than communication to us.

r001.rationale: The response says an overloaded word like “illusions” can carry several distinct concepts at once, such as a possible trap, a mistaken assumption, an adversarial setup, and uncertainty. It presents that compression as why the term persists despite length penalties.

astra-6.text:
I think length penalties push models toward compression, but they don’t necessarily push them toward conceptual precision. A word like “illusion” can stand in for several different ideas: a perceptual error, a misleading intuition, or something that seems real but isn’t. That makes it a cheap way to gesture at an explanation without specifying which claim you’re making.

And if that ambiguity doesn’t get penalized—if the answer still sounds plausible—there’s little pressure to unpack it. You might even make the problem worse with a length penalty, because distinguishing those meanings takes more words. The thing you want to reward is making the right distinction, even when that requires a slightly longer answer.

r001.rationale: The response says “illusion” can stand for several distinct ideas, letting the model gesture at an explanation without specifying which claim it means.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that a length penalty actually favors those terms in some cases. A word like “illusion” can compress a whole bundle of ideas: a misleading appearance, a mistaken belief, a discrepancy between what’s represented and what’s true. Being precise about which one you mean takes more tokens.

So there are two pressures that don’t necessarily line up. You’re penalizing length, but what you really want is conceptual clarity. A model can get shorter by using a loaded abstraction without resolving the ambiguity underneath it. And if that abstraction is common in the language it learned from, it’s a very available shortcut.

I’d want to distinguish whether the term is actually doing useful work from whether it just sounds explanatory. A length penalty alone doesn’t make that distinction.

r001.rationale: The response says “illusion” compresses a bundle of distinct ideas and that this can make the term appealing despite a length penalty.
